queue.tree_name: The Temple Square Cedar of Lebanon
queue.recognise: You can recognise it as an evergreen conifer 20 metres tall on a trunk 277 centimetres round. It stands at the southeast corner of the Salt Lake Temple.
queue.story:
Temple Square's famous cedar is said to have arrived around 1949 in a suitcase, seven inches tall. The Deseret News told its story in 1995: the seedling came in the luggage of a Mrs. Petty of Sugar House and was planted in a corner of the square. Its top was later sheared off, and the gardeners trained a side branch up as a new leader. When the South Visitors' Center was built, the cedar was still marked for removal by oversight; a gardener, Peter Lassig, caught the mistake, and the architect, Emil Fetzer, stopped the crews.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the narrower of two big trees at the southwest corner of Washington Square, its crown about 14 metres across. The broad hackberry stands about 15 metres away.
queue.story:
The taller of the two state champions on this corner of Washington Square is the slim one. Utah's register measured this Ohio buckeye in 2018 at 19.2 metres, almost a metre above the champion hackberry standing about 15 metres away, on a trunk of 213 centimetres and a crown only 13.7 metres across. Two record trees of two different species, on one corner of a city block.

The Ohio buckeye is a Midwestern tree, Ohio's state tree, and a long way from home on the Wasatch Front. Buckeyes are among the first trees to leaf out in spring, opening hand-shaped leaves of five leaflets, then pale yellow-green flower spikes. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 25 metres across on a trunk 373 centimetres round. It stands at the southwest corner of Washington Square, about 15 metres from the narrower, taller Ohio buckeye.
queue.story:
Utah's champion hackberry is wider than it is tall. The state's Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands measured it in 2018 at 18.3 metres high, with a crown spreading 24.7 metres and a trunk 373 centimetres round, and the register lists it as a Heritage Tree as well as the biggest of its species in the state. A hackberry is a tree of the American interior, with warty grey bark and small berries the birds strip in autumn. This one grew into the shape of a shade tree.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its size: a London plane 505 centimetres round and 30.5 metres tall, with a crown about 26 metres across. It stands in Liberty Park, north of the tennis courts.
queue.story:
The biggest London plane in Utah stands north of the tennis courts in Liberty Park, and it is five metres round. The Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands lists it as the state champion of its species and as a Heritage Tree, and its foresters measured it in 2025: a trunk 505 centimetres in circumference, a height of 30.5 metres, and a crown spreading about 26 metres, not far short of its own height.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its several separate stems, once a single trunk that split apart from the 1770s onward, now ringed by a low wall built in 1785 to stop souvenir-taking. It stands inside Fortingall churchyard.
queue.story:
In 2015 a tree that had been male for as long as anyone had recorded it grew berries on a single branch. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh reported the change, and beyond the novelty it was proof that the Fortingall Yew is a working organism rather than a standing relic.

Its age is genuinely disputed and always will be. Forestry and Land Scotland says 5,000 years. Bevan-Jones, the standard academic reference on ancient yews, gives 2,000 to 3,000 and allows that the tree may only date from a post-Roman Christian site here, which would make it around 1,500. Nobody can settle it, because the heartwood rotted out centuries ago and there are no rings left to count.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk 7.2 metres round on a tree only about 12 metres tall, with a small bunch of green in its upper branches. It stands at the top of the Jardine Juniper Trail above Wood Camp.
queue.story:
Hikers will tell you the Jardine Juniper is 3,000 years old. The wood disagrees: cores taken in the 1950s put it at about 1,500, a figure the state's own tourism site repeats. Half the legend is still a very old tree.

Maurice Blood Linford found it in 1923 on a ridge above Logan Canyon and named it after William Marion Jardine. It is not tall, about 12 metres, but the trunk measures 7.2 metres round. At 1,500 years it was already old when the first Europeans reached North America.

queue.tree_name: Dughall Mor and the Reelig Glen giants
queue.recognise: You can recognise the stand as the tallest firs in the glen, close together beside the Moniack Burn path south of the car park, near the information board. Dughall Mor and the Reelig Glen Fir stand about 55 yards apart.
queue.story: Britain's tallest tree lost its title to a neighbour standing about 55 yards away. Both are Douglas firs in Reelig Glen, a wooded glen west of Inverness. The older champion is Dughall Mor, Gaelic for Big Douglas, a name it got from a local competition. It was measured at 62 metres in 2000 and reported at 64 in 2005, and for a while no tree in Britain was known to be taller. Then the Reelig Glen Fir beside it was measured at 66.4 metres in 2014, by laser and by climbing, and reported as the new tallest tree in the UK. Wikipedia's list of superlative trees now gives 66.3 for it and 63.8 for Dughall Mor, which it ranks second. Heights this great shift with method and year, so read it as a close
queue.name: Dughall Mor and the Reelig Glen giants
